'''''Echinopsis oxygona''''', also known as '''Eyries cactus''', '''Easter lily cactus''' or '''sea-urchin cactus''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[cactus]] family Cactaceae, native to south [[Brazil]], [[Uruguay]], [[Paraguay]] and northeastern [[Argentina]].<ref name="Plants of the World Online" /> Some species that have been described separately, including '''''Echinopsis eyriesii''''' and '''''Echinopsis tubiflora''''',<ref name=Ande01>{{Cite book |last=Anderson |first=Edward F. |date=2001 |title=The Cactus Family |publication-place=Pentland, Oregon |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=978-0-88192-498-5 }} Pages 265–266, 285.</ref> are now considered to be [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonymous]].<ref name="Plants of the World Online" /> The features of the species include a large flower, with sharply pointed lavender or white petals, and a sweet scent.

==Description==
''Echinopsis oxygona'' grows singly or in groups. The spherical to short cylindrical, dark green shoots reach heights of up to {{cvt|75|cm}} with a diameter of up to {{cvt|15|cm}}. There are 8 to 18 ribs. The white to tan, gray or black [[areole]]s are up to {{cvt|2|cm}} apart. The [[Thorns, spines, and prickles#Spines|spines]] that emerge from the areoles vary in size and number. In plants that have been treated as ''E. eyriesii'', there are 10–15 very short spines. In plants that have been treated as ''E. oxygona'', the spines are longer: the one to five strong central spines are up to {{cvt|3|–|3.5|cm}} long, and there are up to 20 thinner radial spines up to {{cvt|2.5|cm|1}} long. Plants produce white, lavender or pale red flowers that open at night. The flowers are up to {{cvt|25|cm}} long and up to {{cvt|10|cm}} across.<ref name=Ande01/><ref name="o980">{{cite book | last=Anderson | first=Edward F. | last2=Eggli | first2=Urs | title=Das grosse Kakteen-Lexikon | publisher=Ulmer | publication-place=Stuttgart (Hohenheim) | date=2005 | isbn=3-8001-4573-1 | language=de | page=238}}</ref>

== Habitat ==
''Echinopsis oxygona'', native to Southern Brazil, [[Uruguay]], [[Paraguay]] and [[Entre Ríos Province]], [[Argentina]], thrives in lowland environments, reaching altitudes of up to 1,000 meters above sea level. In these areas, there is a [[tropical climate|tropical]] and [[Continental climate|continental]] climate, characterized by arid winters and humid summers. The annual precipitation in these regions amounts to approximately 1,500 mm, sustaining an average annual temperature range of 25–30°C, rarely dropping below zero degrees.<ref name="llifle">{{Cite web | url=http://www.llifle.com/Encyclopedia/CACTI/Family/Cactaceae/8376/Echinopsis_oxygona |website=Ilife: encyclopedia of living forms; The Encyclopedia of Cacti |title = ''Echinopsis oxygona'' |access-date=8 November 2024}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Echinopsis oxygona'' is known for having huge, showy flowers at the ends of long tubes which are connected to the cactus.  The flower has a sweet smell. The flower opens in the evening and wilts the next afternoon on hot days. It grows well in full sun, or light shade. These cacti can stand strong heat, and even temperatures as low as {{convert|-10|C|F|abbr=on}}. Usually these are outdoor plants. They are used to the dry, desert climate, so they do not need to be watered every day.{{fact|date=September 2023}}

In the 19th century,  ''Echinopsis oxygona'' was extensively hybridized with other ''[[Echinopsis]]'' and ''[[Lobivia]]'' species, giving rise to a number of [[cultivars]] with large colourful flowers.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.llifle.com/Encyclopedia/CACTI/Family/Cactaceae/8004/Echinopsis_eyriesii |website = Ilife: encyclopedia of living forms; The Encyclopedia of Cacti |title=''Echinopsis eyriesii'' (Turpin) Pfeiff. & Otto |access-date=5 December 2024}}</ref>

In cultivation in the UK this plant has received the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/209593/Echinopsis-oxygona/Details | title = ''Echinopsis oxygona'' | website = www.rhs.org | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 5 June 2020}}</ref><gallery>

===Propagation===
Usually, the cactus will start to have small offsets appear at its base.  These can be plucked off and transplanted into a different pot for further growth into a mature cactus. Usually, the cactus will bloom in mid summer. If cultivated away from seasonal temperature changes, the bloom can be initiated any time during the year (assuming sufficient maturity), by watering the cactus after a longer dry period. {{citation needed|date=December 2024}}
